claims.text: A thin, uniform nickel surface coating will reduce molten-aluminum corrosion of boride-based components during hot-dip aluminum plating.
The proposed intervention is a 1–5 µm nickel coating deposited by physical vapor deposition.
The nickel coating will remain continuous on the boride-based substrate during exposure.
A stable interfacial region may form between nickel and the boride-based substrate during molten-aluminum exposure.
Minor nickel aluminide formation may occur at the interface.
The continuous nickel layer will slow or prevent aluminum diffusion into the boride-based substrate.
The nickel coating will limit interdiffusion and chemical reactions between molten aluminum and the underlying boride.
Limiting interdiffusion and chemical reactions will reduce attack and dissolution of the boride phase by molten aluminum.
Nickel-coated components will have lower weight loss than uncoated boride-based components after equivalent molten-aluminum exposure.
Nickel-coated components will exhibit shallower aluminum penetration than uncoated boride-based components.
Nickel-coated components will exhibit less microstructural degradation than uncoated boride-based components.
Untreated boride-based components show measurable corrosion during prolonged exposure to molten aluminum at plating temperatures.
The coating will be effective only while it remains intact and adherent under thermal and chemical stresses.
Extreme thermal cycling or exposure beyond typical service durations may compromise the nickel coating's integrity.
